analysis.one_liner: Replaces private health insurance with a government plan covering every U.S. resident with no premiums, deductibles, or copays.
analysis.headline: A Medicare for All bill backed by 116 of 217 House Democrats has sat in seven committees with no hearings, markups, or votes since its April 2025 introduction.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would create a single national health insurance program run by the Department of Health and Human Services covering all U.S. residents, with no deductibles, copays, coinsurance, or surprise bills. It would cover hospital care, prescription drugs, mental health and addiction treatment, dental, vision, hearing, long-term care, and reproductive and gender-affirming care, and it would require the government to negotiate prescription drug prices. Private insurers could sell only supplemental coverage, employer plans duplicating the program would be banned, and the Obamacare exchanges would be shut down. Benefits would phase in over two years, starting with people under 19 and over 55.
analysis.who_benefits: Every U.S. resident, and most of all people who today pay premiums, deductibles, and copays or go without care because of cost. Uninsured and underinsured people, people with expensive conditions, families paying out of pocket for dental, vision, hearing, or long-term care, and patients who face denials or prior-authorization delays would all get comprehensive coverage with no cost-sharing at the point of care. The bill also offers wage replacement and retraining for workers displaced from health insurance administration jobs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Every U.S. resident, especially the uninsured

how_it_helps.text: Every U.S. resident is covered automatically, including enrollment at birth or upon establishing residency.
No deductibles, copays, coinsurance, or other cost-sharing is allowed, providers cannot balance-bill patients, and care cannot be gated by prior authorization or step-therapy requirements.

The benefits package is comprehensive: hospital care, prescription drugs and devices, mental health and substance use treatment, oral health, audiology, vision, rehabilitative services, hospice, reproductive care including abortion and contraception, gender-affirming care, and long-term services and supports in home and community settings.
HHS must negotiate prescription drug prices, and hospitals would be paid through negotiated global budgets within a national health budget, replacing today's per-case billing.

The Affordable Care Act exchanges and specified federal health programs are sunset when the program is implemented, while Department of Veterans Affairs and Indian Health Service coverage is left in place.
People under 19 and 55 or older can enroll one year after enactment, others can buy in during the transition, and the program is fully implemented two years after enactment.

The bill sets minimum provider standards including nurse-to-patient staffing ratios, applies Medicare fraud-and-abuse sanctions to the whole program, adds provider ethics and financial-conflict-of-interest rules, and protects whistleblowers who report violations.
For up to five years, at least 1% of the program budget goes to wage replacement, retraining, and job placement for workers displaced from health insurance administration and related jobs.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through a new Universal Medicare Trust Fund and a national health budget that would replace the premiums, deductibles, and copays Americans pay today with federal revenue — meaning a substantial tax shift toward businesses and higher earners (the financing title lies beyond the excerpted text, but the Trust Fund and national budget structure is in the bill). Health insurers lose their core business, since selling coverage duplicative of the program becomes unlawful and the exchanges are sunset. Employers lose the ability to provide duplicative health benefits, though they stop paying most premiums. Drug manufacturers face government-negotiated prices.

drawbacks.text: Beginning two years after enactment, it becomes unlawful for private insurers to sell duplicative coverage and for employers to provide benefits duplicating the program, so workers who like their current employer or union plan would lose that option and be moved onto the public plan.

The bill creates a Universal Medicare Trust Fund and a national health budget to pay for care that today is funded by roughly the entire private insurance system plus Medicare and Medicaid — a large transfer of spending onto the federal budget, and the excerpted text does not show the tax title that would raise the revenue.

Hospitals would be paid lump-sum global budgets with a cap on executive compensation and limits on how funds can be used, a system supporters say controls costs but critics warn can squeeze hospital finances and lead to rationing by budget rather than by claim denial.

A single payer with national practice guidelines and coverage determinations would concentrate enormous pricing and coverage power in HHS, and a botched two-year transition could disrupt care networks; the bill itself directs annual reports on 'transition problems' and requires an ombudsman for complaints, an acknowledgment of that risk.
Adding long-term care, dental, vision, and hearing for everyone makes the program substantially more expensive than Medicare today, and the cost is a central argument opponents use against it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For individuals, the benefit is large and direct: no premiums, deductibles, copays, or surprise bills, and coverage today's plans often exclude, like long-term care and full dental and vision. The cost is also large and real: the same health spending moves onto the federal budget as new taxes, and people with employer or union plans they like would lose them for a government plan. The honest trade-off is between a simpler, universal system with government-set prices and the loss of choice among plans plus transition and financing risk. The bill would not add net new health spending so much as replace existing private spending with public spending, but the switch itself is a massive administrative undertaking.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late April 2025 and referred to seven House committees at once, and none of them has held a hearing or advanced it, so it has never come anywhere near a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Pramila Jayapal introduced the Medicare for All Act in the House on April 29, 2025.
116 House Democrats — 116 of the 217 House Democrats — signed on as cosponsors.

The Speaker referred the bill to the Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Education and Workforce, Rules, Oversight and Government Reform, Armed Services, and Judiciary committees, without designating which committee would act first.
The action history shows no hearings, markups, or floor activity since the referral.
Republicans hold a 223-217 majority in the House for this Congress, which runs until January 3, 2027.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, nothing has changed: private insurers, employers, and drug companies keep the current system, and people who remain uninsured or pay high out-of-pocket costs are no better off. If the bill stays parked, the status quo is the winner.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and the status quo, for now

for.name: Rep. Pramila Jayapal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Medicare for All Act and recruited 116 Democratic cosponsors.

against.name: Speaker Mike Johnson
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to seven committees with no lead committee designated, and no committee has taken it up since.

against.name: 223 of 223 House Republicans
against.what_they_did: None cosponsored the bill, and the Republican majority has not scheduled any hearing, markup, or floor vote on it.

against.name: Health insurance and pharmaceutical industry lobbies
against.what_they_did: Have long campaigned against single-payer legislation that would eliminate duplicative private coverage and impose government-negotiated drug prices.

sides.party_line_note: Support is entirely Democratic — 116 of 217 House Democrats cosponsored, zero of 223 Republicans did — and the Republican majority controls the committees and the floor schedule.

industries.note: The core of the industry's business — comprehensive coverage that duplicates the public plan — would become unlawful, and the ACA exchanges would be sunset; insurers could sell only supplemental benefits. Their interest in blocking the bill runs directly against the public's interest in universal no-cost-sharing coverage.

HHS must negotiate prescription drug prices and pay within a national health budget, replacing the current system where manufacturers set prices and insurers pass much of the cost to patients. Their gain from the status quo is patients' cost.
Employers would stop paying the bulk of today's premium bills but would be barred from providing duplicative health benefits, removing a major tool for recruiting and retaining workers.

Universal coverage eliminates uncompensated care and billing overhead, but payment shifts to negotiated global budgets with a compensation cap and limits on capital spending, and executives face financial-conflict-of-interest rules.

Many billing and insurance jobs would disappear as private coverage winds down; the bill sets aside at least 1% of the program budget for up to five years for their wage replacement, retraining, and placement.

analysis.trajectory: With Republicans holding a 223-217 House majority, no Republican support, and the bill parked across seven committees with no lead committee, it will almost certainly not get a hearing, markup, or floor vote before this Congress ends on January 3, 2027. Its realistic role is as a messaging and organizing vehicle — the same fate as prior Medicare for All bills — unless Democrats win both chambers and the presidency in 2026.
